newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan retail chain says closed after bribe demand.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan retail chain says closed after bribe demand.

text.p: One of Kenya's biggest supermarket chains said on Tuesday its stores were ordered closed last week after it refused to pay a massive bribe.

Nakumatt Holdings Ltd took full-page advertisements in Kenyan newspapers to publish a statement saying a mad cow disease scare was a pretext and linking the commerce ministry's closure order with anti-Asian sentiment.
Commerce Minister Kirugi M'Mukindia will address a news conference on the affair on Wednesday, his ministry said, adding it had no comment to make until then.

Nakumatt's eight stores in Kenya were closed on September 19 when the ministry revoked its trading licences on grounds it imported without proper approval corned beef from Britain which has had outbreaks of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) or "mad cow" disease.

Nakumatt said an anonymous caller telephoned Nakumatt on September 17 and 19 demanding a payment of 50 million shillings ($893,000) in return for solving "the purported canned beef problem". Nakumatt said it refused and the caller warned the company it would incur heavy penalties.
"The reason for the closure of our stores throughout Kenya can only be attributed to the anonymous caller and the money that had earlier been asked for," Nakumatt's statement said.
It said Nakumatt staff had received death threats in the past three days.
It said the corned beef was from Brazil and packed there by British company John West and then exported to Kenya.
John West confirmed this in a statement issued in London.
"Locally reared beef is used by our Brazilian supplier and this is not in any way associated with BSE," it said. "There is no reason why this consignment should be held," John West said.
Nakumatt is owned by Kenyan Asians, migrants from the Indian sub-continent who first came to East Africa in large numbers during British colonial rule and now dominate the retail sector.

The company's statement linked the closure of the stores with periodic campaigns by Kenyan politicians of African origin to greatly reduce the size of the Asian population by "besmirching and sometimes expelling members of the Asian business community".
